title: Performance & Indexing
tagline: Storage engine internals — vacuum & bloat, buffer cache, read amplification, and PL/pgSQL at scale

blocks.md: Plans are only half the story — storage layout decides the other half. Vacuum health, cache behavior, and index-only scans are where real PostgreSQL tuning lives.

blocks.text: MVCC: rows are never edited in place

blocks.md: PostgreSQL does not update a heap tuple in place. An UPDATE writes a brand-new row version and leaves the old one available to transactions that might still see it; once no transaction can, the old version is a dead tuple. Dead tuples waste space, slow sequential scans (more pages to visit), and bloat indexes. Autovacuum is the background janitor: it removes dead tuples, advances the visibility map, refreshes statistics, and prevents transaction-id wraparound. It wakes on a schedule (autovacuum_naptime) and triggers per table from dead-tuple counts and scale factors. You tune those knobs for churn — you never switch autovacuum off.

blocks.label: seeing vacuum pressure
blocks.pg:
-- Per table: ALTER TABLE orders SET (autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.05);
-- autovacuum_vacuum_threshold is the absolute minimum dead-tuple count
blocks.mysql: -- InnoDB: no autovacuum concept — purge threads reap old row versions asynchronously
blocks.py-pandas: # pandas has no vacuum; copy the live frame to drop deleted rows

blocks.md: **Don't disable autovacuum.** It is the only thing stopping unconstrained table growth and transaction-id wraparound. For a heavy-churn table, tune it per table — lower `autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor` (e.g. 0.05) or raise `autovacuum_vacuum_cost_limit` so the worker finishes faster — instead of freezing it.

items.q: Frequent UPDATEs send n_dead_tup climbing in pg_stat_user_tables. The right habit is…
options: Let autovacuum work; tune scale_factor/threshold for heavy churn
items.explain: MVCC appends new row versions; dead tuples accumulate until autovacuum — or manual VACUUM — reclaims them.

items.q: The pg_stat_user_tables columns that expose vacuum pressure are…
items.explain: n_live_tup / n_dead_tup are the direct live-vs-dead census that autovacuum uses to decide when to act.

blocks.title: EXPLAIN ANALYZE UPDATE — a new row version, not an in-place edit (MVCC)

blocks.md: Every heap page and index page is 8KB of storage. Read amplification is how many pages a query must pull in to answer it: an index lookup walks root → branch → leaf → heap row, and a bad plan turns a handful of reads into millions. The first line of defense is shared_buffers — PostgreSQL's in-memory page cache. A hot table that already sits in shared_buffers costs nothing: a sequential scan of it is memory reads, not disk I/O. The number that matters is the cache hit ratio — pages served from memory over total pages read — not the scan type. Throwing a cold multi-GB scan at the cache evicts hot pages (their pg_buffercache usagecount drops), starving the workload that actually pays the bills.

blocks.label: inspecting the buffer pool
blocks.code:
-- How big is the buffer pool?
SHOW shared_buffers;

-- How many pages of the orders heap are resident in memory right now?
SELECT count(*) AS resident_pages
FROM pg_buffercache
WHERE relfilenode = 'orders'::regclass;

-- Which relations dominate the cache, and how hot are they?
SELECT c.relname,
       count(*) AS pages,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE b.isdirty) AS dirty,
       max(b.usagecount) AS hottest_usage
FROM pg_buffercache b
JOIN pg_class c ON c.relfilenode = b.relfilenode
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY pages DESC
LIMIT 10;

items.q: Why can a sequential scan of a small hot table be perfectly healthy?
options: Its pages already live in shared_buffers — the cache hit ratio, not the scan type, is the metric
items.explain: If every page read is a shared_buffers hit, the scan is RAM-speed regardless of the plan node.

blocks.text: Index Only Scan — the visibility map decides

blocks.md: A plain btree index returns row pointers; fetching the actual row from the heap is the expensive tail. An Index Only Scan reverses that: if every column the query needs is IN the index (key columns + INCLUDE payload) AND the heap page is all-visible, PostgreSQL returns the index entry directly — Heap Fetches: 0. 'All-visible' is a per-page fact recorded in the visibility map, and only VACUUM/autovacuum marks pages all-visible. On pages still being touched — or not yet vacuumed — the planner must fetch the heap tuple to double-check visibility; EXPLAIN then shows Heap Fetches > 0 and the covering advantage quietly evaporates.

blocks.label: covering index
blocks.code:
-- Key columns drive the scan; amount rides along as payload
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_status_ts
  ON orders (status, created_at) INCLUDE (amount);

-- All needed columns are in the index → eligible for Index Only Scan
EXPLAIN SELECT amount
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'paid' AND created_at > now() - interval '7 days';
blocks.pg:
-- EXPLAIN ANALYZE: 'Heap Fetches: 0' = visibility map cooperated
-- Heap Fetches > 0 = pages not all-visible; vacuum refreshes the map
blocks.mysql:
-- MySQL 8.0: no INCLUDE — covering index = all columns in the key
-- EXPLAIN shows 'Using index' when fully covered

items.q: EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows Index Only Scan ... Heap Fetches: 3200. Why are there heap fetches?
options: Some heap pages are not all-visible, so rows must be checked against the heap
The index has no INCLUDE columns
items.explain: Heap Fetches > 0 means the visibility map doesn't cover those pages yet; autovacuum refreshes it and fetches trend toward 0.

blocks.title: Index Only Scan using idx_orders_status_ts — visibility map clean → Heap Fetches: 0
Index Only Scan using idx_orders_status_ts — stale visibility map → Heap Fetches > 0 (vacuum to fix)

blocks.text: fillfactor — page headroom is a policy decision

blocks.md: The default heap fillfactor is 100: every new page is packed full. That is fine for append-only loads but painful for UPDATE-heavy tables — an updated row that no longer fits its page is relocated, splitting pages and damaging locality. fillfactor = 70 reserves 30% of each page so short updates stay in place. It is a trade: more pages per table and slightly longer scans, in exchange for far less physical churn. The setting only affects new pages — existing pages keep their old packing until a rewrite. Index pages already default to fillfactor 90 for the same reason: room to insert without splitting.

-- Rewrite needed to re-pack pages written before the fillfactor change
blocks.mysql: -- InnoDB has no per-table fillfactor; OPTIMIZE TABLE rebuilds to reclaim space

blocks.md: **Reorganize when bloat is real.** free_percent much above ~30% means the table is mostly holes. Options: `VACUUM FULL` rewrites and compacts but takes an AccessExclusive lock (writes block); `pg_repack` rewrites online behind a shadow table; CTAS into a fresh table and swap achieves the same offline. Plain `VACUUM` frees space for reuse but does not shrink the file.

items.q: What does fillfactor = 70 buy an UPDATE-heavy table?
options: Room in each page so short updates stay in-page (HOT) instead of relocating
items.explain: Lower fillfactor keeps updated rows in their original page — fewer relocations, splits, and index churn.

blocks.text: Plan caching: the hidden performance lever

blocks.md: PL/pgSQL caches the *plan template* per statement/key. A **one-size-fits-all plan** stays cached for the session — great for uniform workloads, a trap for skewed values. Parameters matter: generic plans win when statistics say the same plan fits all inputs; custom plans win on skew.

blocks.md: **Prepared plans go stale**: after bulk loads or schema changes the cached plan's row estimates are wrong. Watch for 'generic plan' with wildly off row counts in procs and re-prepare or bump `plan_cache_mode`.

items.q: A PROCEDURE differs from a FUNCTION in pg because it:
items.explain: Top-level transaction control (COMMIT) is only allowed in PROCEDURE bodies, never inside a FUNCTION called from a query.

items.q: Prepared/plan-cached generic plans are dangerous when:
options: Inputs are heavily skewed and the plan is one-size-fits-all
items.explain: A single cached plan optimized for an average value mis-executes on outliers — consider custom plans for skewed keys.

blocks.md: PostgreSQL, MySQL 8.0 InnoDB, and SQL Server all reclaim dead storage eventually — the verbs differ. PostgreSQL: autovacuum on a tunable schedule plus explicit VACUUM, visibility maps, per-table tuning, pgstat views. MySQL: record-level purge runs inside InnoDB (purge threads), and you compact explicitly — OPTIMIZE TABLE rebuilds the table, information_schema.tables.data_free reports reclaimable bytes. SQL Server exposes a fill-factor knob (FILLFACTOR) as an index option to keep page headroom — the same idea as a low heap fillfactor. The vocabulary differs; the goal — compact storage so reads stay cheap — is shared.

blocks.sql:
-- Storage hygiene: reclaim dead versions of rows
VACUUM ANALYZE orders;
blocks.py-pandas: # Filter out deleted rows: df = df[df['deleted'].isna()]

-- SQL Server: same knob, index option
CREATE INDEX i ON t (c) WITH (FILLFACTOR = 70);

CREATE INDEX i ON t (c) WITH (fillfactor = 90); -- btree default is 90

items.title: Autovacuum Tuning Proposal
items.statement: A table of ~2M rows churns 20% of its live tuples every day; pg_stat_user_tables shows n_dead_tup climbing toward 400k between autovacuum runs. Propose per-table autovacuum settings (scale_factor / threshold), justify them with the pg_stat numbers, and say what else you would verify before touching the query.
hints: Lower autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor (e.g. 0.05) so a smaller dead-tuple fraction triggers a sweep
autovacuum_vacuum_threshold is the absolute minimum dead-tuple count before autovacuum acts
autovacuum_vacuum_cost_limit / autovacuum_naptime control how aggressively the background worker runs

items.title: Measure Table Bloat
items.statement: orders has grown to roughly 3x its logical size. Write the pgstattuple_approx invocation to measure free_percent, interpret the value, and choose between plain VACUUM, VACUUM FULL, and pg_repack — explaining the lock trade-off of each.
hints: CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pgstattuple; SELECT free_percent FROM pgstattuple_approx('orders');
free_percent well above ~30% justifies a rewrite (VACUUM FULL / pg_repack / CTAS)
VACUUM FULL rewrites and compacts but takes an AccessExclusive lock; pg_repack rewrites online

items.title: Covering Index to Kill Heap Fetches
items.statement: A hot dashboard runs SELECT amount FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' AND created_at > now() - interval '7 days' thousands of times a minute; EXPLAIN ANALYZE reports Index Only Scan ... Heap Fetches: 3800. Design the covering index, explain why Heap Fetches should approach 0, and when the visibility map still matters.
hints: CREATE INDEX idx_orders_status_ts ON orders (status, created_at) INCLUDE (amount);
Index Only Scan still needs pages all-visible — VACUUM/autovacuum maintain the visibility map
Heap Fetches > 0 signals not-all-visible pages, not a wrong index

items.title: Buffer Cache Arithmetic
items.statement: shared_buffers = 8GB. The hot working set is 12GB (orders + recent activity) plus hundreds of GB of cold history. Reason about the cache-hit ratio: what would you cache first, and what happens to pg_buffercache.usagecount when a periodic full scan of the cold history table runs?
hints: CacheHitRatio = pages served from memory over total pages read — hits are RAM-speed, misses are disk I/O
A small hot table: thousands of resident pages in shared_buffers means every read is a hit
A periodic cold scan evicts hot pages (usagecount drops toward 1); batch it or shrink its footprint

items.title: Stored-Procedure Cost Audit
items.statement: Audit a PL/pgSQL function for planner-friendliness. Findings to confirm: (1) no volatility marker — it should be STABLE; (2) it calls a user-defined function declared VOLATILE inside WHERE, defeating index use; (3) it is invoked through a cached generic plan with skewed inputs. Explain each cost to the planner and the fixes.
hints: Mark functions STABLE/IMMUTABLE where accurate so the planner can constant-fold and reuse the plan
VOLATILE functions in WHERE force per-row evaluation — the planner cannot simplify or index-probe the predicate
Skewed inputs + a one-size-fits-all cached plan → wrong estimates; check plan_cache_mode or re-prepare

revisionCard: Dead tuples: MVCC appends new row versions on UPDATE; autovacuum reclaims them — tune scale_factor/threshold for churn, never disable it
Index-Only Scan triad: covering columns in the index + visibility map marks the page all-visible → Heap Fetches: 0
fillfactor: leave page headroom (e.g. 70) so short UPDATEs stay in-page (HOT); setting affects only new pages
Bloat path: pgstattuple_approx → free_percent; rewrite via VACUUM FULL (lock) or pg_repack (online)
Cache: CacheHitRatio + pg_buffercache.usagecount; a hot small table against shared_buffers reads from memory, not disk
PL/pgSQL: STABLE/IMMUTABLE markers; volatile calls in WHERE defeat the planner; cached generic plans go stale on skewed input

glossary.def: Multi-version concurrency control: writers append new row versions instead of overwriting, so readers never block writers.
Old row version no longer visible to any transaction; reclaimed by VACUUM/autovacuum.
Dead space in table or index pages from row churn that has not been reclaimed or repacked.
Per-heap-page bits marking pages where every row version is visible to everyone — enables index-only scans and cheap VACUUM.
Answering a query from index entries alone; requires all needed columns in the index and all-visible heap pages (Heap Fetches: 0).
Index whose key + INCLUDE payload holds every column a query needs, removing heap fetches.
Per-table (and per-index) page fill policy; leaving headroom keeps UPDATEs in-page and reduces relocation.
Fraction of page reads served from memory; the leading indicator for whether tuning should focus on caching or on reducing reads.
